articles.title: People with psychosis and a history of aggression are more likely to mistake negative emotions for positive ones
articles.summary: Misreading another person’s irritation or sadness as something positive could mean missing a cue to back off. A new study found this error was more common in people with psychotic disorders and a history of aggression.

articles.title: Expecting to lose economic standing hurts well-being more than expecting to gain helps it
articles.summary: Worrying about slipping down the socioeconomic ladder may take a psychological toll. Across four studies in Spain and the U.S., expecting downward mobility was tied to greater status anxiety, which in turn predicted lower life satisfaction.

articles.title: Breast reduction surgery is linked to improved sexual function
articles.summary: A new meta-analysis reveals that breast reduction surgery is linked to improvements in sexual desire, arousal, and satisfaction. Researchers suggest that alleviating physical pain and reducing appearance-related anxiety both play a role in enhancing postoperative sexual well-being.

articles.title: Emotional struggles are linked to vulnerable narcissism but not grandiose narcissism, meta-analysis finds
articles.summary: A meta-analysis of 26 studies involving more than 12,000 adults found that vulnerable narcissism was moderately linked to difficulty managing emotions, while grandiose narcissism showed virtually no connection.

articles.title: The psychology behind Taylor Swift’s billion-dollar media empire
articles.summary: The intense, one-sided connections fans feel toward Taylor Swift and their fear of missing out strongly predict whether they will attend her concerts and movies, highlighting how the psychological need for social belonging drives massive consumer behaviors.

articles.title: Psychopathy scores run a bit higher among Americans still living in their home state, study finds
articles.summary: Americans who still live in the state where they grew up score slightly higher on psychopathy than those who moved away, according to a study of nearly 4,000 adults. The gap was small but persisted in the strictest comparisons.

articles.title: Breakthrough PTSD treatment achieves 68% remission rate in clinical trial
articles.summary: A newly FDA-cleared PTSD treatment uses personalized brain mapping and magnetic stimulation to target abnormal brain activity, with a clinical trial reporting a 52% reduction in symptoms and 68% remission. Researchers believe the technology could transform PTSD care and pave the way for more precise treatments for other mental health conditions.

articles.title: Scientists discover a hidden messaging system deep inside the brain
articles.summary: A tiny region deep within the brain has surprised scientists by revealing a remarkably sophisticated communication system. Previously thought to broadcast the same chemical signal throughout the brain, this region actually sends targeted messages that help control learning, attention, and behavior, according to new research in mice.

articles.title: Millions take fish oil for brain health. A two-year study found no benefit
articles.summary: A surprising two-year clinical trial found that fish oil supplements successfully delivered omega-3s to the brain but failed to improve memory or protect against Alzheimer's-related brain shrinkage. Researchers suspect that getting these nutrients through a healthy diet may offer benefits that supplements alone cannot provide.

articles.title: Scientists discover a surprising secret behind the human brain’s wrinkles
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered why common marmosets have unusually small, smooth brains despite starting development much like other primates. The secret lies in subtle changes to brain-building cells that slow neuron production, revealing new clues about how the large, folded human brain evolved.

articles.title: Do people become less creative as they get older? Research makes surprising discovery
articles.summary: Study pitting preschoolers against adults mostly in their 20s finds fear of failure and anxiety hamper the grownups Ask a five-year-old to paint a picture and they will almost instinctively reach for the brush, but ask an adult to do the same and they will often hesitate and shy away. Now researchers say they know why. While it is widely assumed children are more creative than adults, a new study challenges this…

articles.summary: Research shows how seeing bigger violations by others can lead people to increase their own rule-breaking From politicians taking bribes to bullying and harassment in City firms , leaders have been quick to label those who break the rules as the odd “bad apple”. But new research backs up the idiom that one bad apple can spoil the barrel. Researchers have found that when people go beyond the rule-breaking they see in…

articles.title: Your aging brain may be trading memory for something more valuable
articles.summary: The aging brain may be undergoing a remarkable transformation rather than simply losing its abilities, shifting its focus from remembering details to understanding the bigger picture. Scientists suggest this change could be an evolutionary adaptation that helps older adults develop wisdom and share decades of knowledge with younger generations.

articles.title: Ultrasonic technology enables earlier stress-fracture detection
articles.summary: Tibial stress fractures are among the most common overuse injuries affecting military personnel, but they can be difficult to identify in their earliest stages. Small stresses in the bone may develop before an injury becomes apparent through conventional diagnostic tools, creating a window of opportunity for earlier detection to enable intervention.

articles.title: 10 years after Ebola in West Africa: Laboratory partnership improves viral hemorrhagic fever diagnostics in Guinea
articles.summary: Drawing on nearly a decade of surveillance, the researchers document the burden of Lassa fever in the region and explain how sustainable diagnostic structures can support prevention and help reduce the risk of major viral outbreaks.

articles.title: Triple-action weekly weight-loss drug reduces sleep apnea in two late-stage trials
articles.summary: Sleep apnea often gets passed off as mere snoring, but it's a much bigger deal. Throughout the night, breathing keeps pausing, and each pause chips away at sleep quality. Left untreated, repeated breathing disruptions and drops in blood oxygen during sleep can do far more than leave you groggy in the morning—they can take a serious toll on long-term health.

articles.title: Could lowering high blood pressure be as simple as stimulating your ear?
articles.summary: A small device that gently stimulates nerves through the ear could offer a new way to tackle stubborn high blood pressure. In a clinical trial of 63 patients already taking medication, the treatment proved safe, easy to use at home, and well tolerated. Although it did not significantly outperform a placebo overall, patients with more severe hypertension showed promising reductions in blood pressure.

articles.title: Creating 'satellite maps' of thousands of proteins across tissue could transform drug therapies
articles.summary: Much like a satellite provides a full picture of Earth, a new technology can generate thousands of detailed "satellite maps" showing where individual proteins are located and distributed across an entire tissue in the body or brain.

articles.title: Your blood could reveal inflammatory bowel disease 10 years before diagnosis
articles.summary: A major study has uncovered hidden warning signs of inflammatory bowel disease in the blood up to 10 years before diagnosis. Researchers discovered distinct antibody patterns that could help predict who would later develop Crohn’s disease or ulcerative colitis, even distinguishing people at risk of more complicated disease.

articles.title: Scientists discover a hidden switch that burns fat and blocks new fat cells
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered that switching off a protein called Mitch makes human cells burn more fat and prevents new fat cells from developing. The breakthrough builds on experiments in mice that showed remarkable resistance to obesity and improved muscular endurance, raising hopes for a new approach to weight-loss treatment.

articles.title: Ebola vaccine trial begins in DR Congo

articles.title: Glioblastoma breakthrough reveals how brain cancer cells become more aggressive
articles.summary: Scientists discovered that the thick, sticky fluid surrounding glioblastoma tumors can make brain cancer cells smaller, more flexible, and better at invading surrounding tissue. Even more troubling, some of these changes persist after the cells leave the thick fluid, revealing a previously overlooked mechanism that could help this deadly cancer spread.
